error_modes.label: Altitude control through the position change

texts.0: SP, due to back pressure released while unloading the aircraft to move aft and under the leader, did not hold the formation altitude during the position change. The result was a descent of more than 300 feet below the formation altitude, developed inside the crossing and not arrested. The IP took the controls to stop the sink and to reposition the aircraft in the formation.
texts.1: SP, due to a pitch input that was not coordinated with the power reduction, did not keep the formation altitude while crossing behind the leader. Altitude reached the 300 feet limit low, and the deviation stopped growing only after repeated verbal indications from the IP. The recovery to the formation altitude was slow and required a second prompt.
texts.2: SP, due to a power reduction applied without the matching pitch correction, did not hold altitude constant through the crossing. Altitude deviated between 150 and 300 feet below the formation altitude at the aft point of the maneuver. SP recognized the trend on the altimeter, corrected it in time and re-established the formation altitude without any intervention.
texts.3: SP held the formation altitude throughout the cross under, with deviation contained inside 150 feet. Pitch and power inputs were coordinated as the aircraft moved aft, across and back up into position. Any excursion was detected and corrected at once.
texts.4: SP completed the whole position change with negligible altitude excursion, effectively unchanged from the formation altitude and far inside the 150 feet band. Pitch control remained precise while the visual reference shifted from one side of the leader to the other, and no correction of the vertical position was needed after stabilization.
texts.marginal: SP stayed inside the altitude standards during the cross under, but on two crossings the deviation approached the tighter 150 feet band and always on the low side under the leader. The trend indicates that back pressure is relaxed as SP moves aft, and that the recovery of altitude is left to the end of the maneuver. Expected improvement is to hold the vertical position within a stable narrow band from the start to the completion of the crossing.

error_modes.label: Airspeed control during the aft displacement and the rejoin

texts.0: SP, due to a power reduction far larger than the one required to generate the aft displacement, did not control the airspeed during the position change. The result was a loss of more than 20 knots against the briefed formation airspeed and an uncontrolled drop well behind the leader. The IP intervened on the throttle and on the controls to recover the position.
texts.1: SP, due to a power correction applied only after the separation was already visible, did not keep the airspeed inside the formation band. The deviation reached 20 knots below the formation airspeed and was reduced only after verbal indications from the IP on the power setting. The rejoin to the new position was completed late.
texts.2: SP, due to a late reduction and a late restoration of power around the crossing, did not keep the airspeed constant during the position change. The deviation stayed between 10 and 20 knots from the formation airspeed. SP recognized the closure difference in good time, adjusted power and stabilized the airspeed without any intervention.
texts.3: SP controlled the airspeed inside 10 knots of the formation airspeed for the whole cross under. Power was reduced by the amount needed for the aft displacement and restored in time for the rejoin, so that closure remained controlled. Stabilization in the new position was achieved without airspeed hunting.
texts.4: SP flew the position change with negligible airspeed excursion, well inside the 10 knots band and with power inputs of the exact size required. The aft displacement, the crossing and the rejoin were flown with a continuously matched closure rate. No airspeed correction was necessary after the new position was reached.
texts.marginal: SP kept the airspeed inside the standards during the cross under, but the deviation repeatedly approached 10 knots low on the aft displacement. The trend is toward an initial power reduction slightly larger than needed, which is then compensated at the rejoin. Expected improvement is to size the power reduction so that the airspeed variation remains small and symmetrical about the formation airspeed.

error_modes.label: Heading on completion of the crossing

texts.0: SP, due to a bank input toward the new side that was not removed once the lateral displacement had been achieved, did not stabilize on the leader's heading at the completion of the crossing. The result was a divergence of more than 10 degrees from the formation heading with continued lateral travel away from the leader. The IP intervened on the controls to stop the divergence and to re-establish the position.
texts.1: SP, due to a delayed removal of the crossing bank, did not roll out on the formation heading at the end of the position change. The heading divergence reached 10 degrees and was reduced only after verbal indications from the IP. Alignment with the leader was regained late and with a second correction.
texts.2: SP, due to a rollout started after the aircraft had already reached the new lateral position, did not settle on the formation heading immediately. The divergence remained between 5 and 10 degrees. SP recognized the misalignment against the leader, corrected it promptly and stabilized on the formation heading without any intervention.
texts.3: SP completed the crossing aligned with the leader, with heading divergence contained inside 5 degrees. The bank used for the lateral displacement was removed at the correct point so that the aircraft arrived on the new side already tracking the formation heading. No further heading correction was required after stabilization.
texts.4: SP arrived in the new position with negligible heading divergence, effectively parallel to the leader and far inside the 5 degrees band. The lateral displacement was stopped exactly at the required point, and the aircraft tracked the formation heading from the moment of arrival. Lateral position remained constant without further inputs.
texts.marginal: SP finished the crossings inside the heading standards, but the divergence at the rollout repeatedly approached 5 degrees, always in the direction of travel. The trend indicates that the bank is held slightly beyond the point where the new lateral position has been reached. Expected improvement is to anticipate the rollout so that the aircraft arrives on the new side already aligned with the leader.

error_modes.label: Timely and correct execution of the position change on the leader's command

texts.0: SP, due to distraction by a secondary cockpit task during a critical phase of flight, did not execute the position change timely and correctly on the leader's command. The result was an initiation of the crossing several seconds after the signal and in the wrong direction, with the aircraft displaced toward the leader instead of aft. The IP intervened on the controls to stop the movement and to complete the change of position.
texts.1: SP, due to distraction by radio traffic while established in the formation, did not begin the position change at the time required by the leader's command. The crossing was started only after repeated verbal indications from the IP and after the leader had already been established in the new configuration. The sequence was then flown correctly but out of phase with the flight.
texts.2: SP, due to a short lapse in the visual scan of the leader after the command, did not initiate the position change at the exact moment of the signal. The result was a delay of a few seconds at the start of the crossing. SP recognized the delay, executed the remaining sequence in the correct order and completed the change of position without any intervention.
texts.3: SP executed the position change timely and correctly on the leader's command, without any need for IP intervention. The signal was acknowledged and the aft displacement, the crossing and the rejoin were flown in the correct sequence. The new position was established within the expected time.
texts.4: SP executed every position change immediately on the leader's command and in the exact briefed sequence, with no prompting of any kind. The response to the signal was instantaneous and the crossing was completed in a single continuous movement. The result was a change of position that matched the leader's expectation without any correction.
texts.marginal: SP executed the position changes on the leader's command within standards, but the initiation was consistently one to two seconds behind the signal. The trend is toward waiting for confirmation of the command before acting, which lengthens the time spent in transit. Expected improvement is to respond to the leader's signal immediately and to keep the whole sequence continuous.

error_modes.label: Longitudinal spacing within one aircraft length

texts.0: SP, due to a closure rate that was not controlled with small power corrections during the aft displacement, did not keep the spacing from the leader inside one aircraft length. The result was a separation of several aircraft lengths, with the leader's aspect no longer usable as a formation reference. The IP took the controls to re-establish the position.
texts.1: SP, due to power corrections applied only after the separation had become visible, did not hold the spacing within the required limit. Distance from the leader reached one aircraft length during the crossing and was reduced only after verbal indications from the IP. The rejoin to the new position was completed late and with excessive closure.
texts.2: SP, due to an initial power reduction slightly larger than required for the displacement, did not keep the spacing constant through the crossing. The separation grew toward one aircraft length at the aft point of the maneuver. SP recognized the increasing aspect change in time, restored power and closed the spacing without any intervention.
texts.3: SP kept the spacing from the leader inside one aircraft length throughout the cross under. Power was used in small corrections so that the aft displacement remained the minimum needed to clear the leader. The new position was reached with the correct longitudinal reference established.
texts.4: SP maintained the spacing from the leader essentially constant and well inside one aircraft length for the whole position change. The aft displacement was limited to what was needed for clearance and was recovered without overshoot. The formation references remained continuously usable at every point of the crossing.
texts.marginal: SP remained within the spacing limit during the cross under, but on each crossing the separation approached one aircraft length before being closed. The trend is toward using distance rather than precise power control to secure clearance from the leader. Expected improvement is to keep the aft displacement small and to control it with early, small power corrections.

error_modes.label: Avoidance of the leader's prop wash during the crossing

texts.0: SP, due to an insufficient step down when passing behind the leader, did not keep the aircraft clear of the leader's prop wash. The result was entry into the wash with an uncommanded roll and a loss of the visual reference on the leader. The IP took the controls to recover the aircraft and to re-establish separation from the formation.
texts.1: SP, due to a vertical displacement started only after the aircraft had begun to move aft, did not avoid the edge of the leader's prop wash. The aircraft was buffeted while crossing and the step down was increased only after verbal indications from the IP. The remaining crossing was completed with delay and with the reference on the leader partly lost.
texts.2: SP, due to a step down established slightly late relative to the aft displacement, did not maintain the full vertical clearance from the leader's wake. The result was a brief light buffet at the closest point of the crossing. SP recognized the indication at once, increased the step down and completed the crossing clear of the wash without any intervention.
texts.3: SP kept the aircraft clear of the leader's prop wash for the whole position change. The step down was established before the aft displacement and was held until the aircraft was clear on the new side. No buffet was encountered and the visual reference on the leader was retained throughout.
texts.4: SP crossed under the leader with a vertical clearance that was correct and stable at every point, and no trace of wake was encountered. The step down was established early, held exactly as needed and recovered smoothly on arrival in the new position. The reference on the leader was maintained continuously and the crossing was flown in one uninterrupted movement.
texts.marginal: SP avoided the leader's prop wash on all crossings, but the step down was established only marginally before the aft displacement began. The trend is toward a vertical clearance that is adequate rather than comfortable at the closest point of the crossing. Expected improvement is to set the step down earlier and to hold it constant until the aircraft is fully clear on the new side.

error_modes.label: Minimum separation of 10 feet from No1

texts.0: SP, due to a perceptual error in judging closure and lateral separation, did not respect the minimum distance from No1 during the crossing. The result was an approach closer than 10 feet to the leader with continuing closure and no corrective input. The IP took the controls to open the separation and to terminate the maneuver.
texts.1: SP, due to a perceptual error in judging closure while the leader's aspect was changing, did not keep the separation from No1 at a safe value. The distance reached the 10 feet limit and was opened only after an immediate verbal call from the IP. The position change was then completed with the reference on the leader regained late.
texts.2: SP, due to a misjudged closure rate at the start of the lateral displacement, did not maintain the planned separation from No1. The distance reduced noticeably toward the leader before stabilizing well above 10 feet. SP recognized the closure early, arrested it with a small lateral correction and completed the crossing without any intervention.
texts.3: SP kept the separation from No1 comfortably greater than 10 feet at every point of the position change. Closure was controlled with small, early inputs and the lateral displacement was stopped exactly where required. The crossing was completed with the safety margin from the leader preserved throughout.
texts.4: SP flew the whole position change with a separation from No1 that was never in question, far above the 10 feet minimum and constant at every phase. Closure was anticipated rather than corrected, and the aircraft was placed in the new position with a steady lateral margin. No convergence toward the leader developed at any stage.
texts.marginal: SP kept the separation from No1 above the minimum on every crossing, but the lateral margin reduced more than necessary at the point of passing under the leader. The trend indicates that the closure is judged late and then stopped with a single correction. Expected improvement is to assess the closure rate earlier so that the lateral margin remains comfortable and constant during the crossing.

error_modes.label: Smooth, continuous and solid aircraft control

texts.0: SP, due to an over-controlled aircraft (AE104) in the correction, did not control the aircraft in a smooth, continuous and solid manner during the cross under. The result was a sustained lateral oscillation about the intended path, with successive inputs that amplified rather than damped the movement. The IP took the controls to stabilize the aircraft and to establish it in the new position.
texts.1: SP, due to control inputs of excessive size applied in response to each visual change, did not fly the position change smoothly and continuously. The aircraft moved in a series of abrupt steps and the oscillation stopped only after verbal indications from the IP on the size of the inputs. Stabilization in the new position was reached late.
texts.2: SP, due to an initial control input larger than the displacement required, did not keep the movement continuous at the start of the crossing. The result was an abrupt beginning followed by a small overshoot of the intended path. SP reduced the size of the subsequent inputs, damped the movement and completed the crossing smoothly without any intervention.
texts.3: SP controlled the aircraft in a smooth, continuous and solid manner throughout the position change. Control inputs were proportionate to the displacement required and the aircraft moved along one continuous path from the old to the new position. No overshoot or oscillation developed at any stage.
texts.4: SP flew the position change as a single continuous movement, with control inputs so measured that no correction of the path was necessary. The aircraft was placed in the new position with a positive, solid stop and no residual oscillation. Control precision was maintained even while the visual reference on the leader changed side.
texts.marginal: SP flew the cross under within the control standards, but each crossing began with an input slightly larger than needed and was followed by a small damping correction. The trend indicates a step-wise rather than a continuous displacement. Expected improvement is to size the initial input to the required displacement so that the aircraft moves along one smooth path and stops positively in the new position.

error_modes.label: Establishing the small forward LOS rate that starts the aft displacement

texts.0: SP, due to the initial power reduction being omitted at the start of the cross under, did not establish the small forward LOS rate that produces the aft displacement. The lateral movement toward the new side was begun from the fingertip position with no nose-tail clearance built up, and the aircraft was allowed to approach No1 closer than 10 feet while still nearly abeam. The IP took the controls to stop the lateral movement and to open the separation from the leader.
texts.1: SP, due to a power reduction too small to generate any usable forward LOS rate, did not move aft before starting to cross behind the leader. Separation from No1 reduced to the 10 feet limit with the leader still abeam, and the aft displacement was created only after verbal indications from the IP on the throttle. The crossing was completed late and with the clearance regained rather than planned.
texts.2: SP, due to a power reduction applied after the lateral movement had already started, established the small forward LOS rate late in the sequence. Nose-tail clearance was therefore still building while the aircraft was moving toward the leader, and the spacing gained aft stayed below the intended one aircraft length reference. SP recognized the leader's aspect, held the lateral movement until clearance was achieved and completed the crossing without any intervention.
texts.3: SP reduced power as required to establish a small forward LOS rate before any lateral movement was made. The aft displacement developed first, so that the crossing behind the leader was flown with spacing inside one aircraft length and with separation from No1 clearly greater than 10 feet. The sequence of aft displacement, crossing and rejoin was flown in the correct order.
texts.4: SP established a forward LOS rate of exactly the size needed, using a power reduction of a few percent torque, and let the aft displacement build before any bank was applied. Nose-tail clearance was achieved with negligible loss of the formation reference and the separation from No1 never came near the 10 feet minimum. No further adjustment of the longitudinal position was required during the crossing.
texts.marginal: SP produced a forward LOS rate on each cross under, but on repeated attempts the lateral movement was started while the aft displacement was still developing. Spacing and separation remained inside the standards, yet the clearance behind the leader was consistently at the low end of what the technique calls for. Expected improvement is to reduce power first, let the small forward LOS rate build the nose-tail clearance, and only then begin the lateral displacement.

error_modes.label: Sizing the power reduction when the cross under is flown in a climb

texts.0: SP, due to a full-sized power reduction applied while the formation was climbing, did not limit the rearward movement generated during the cross under. Excessive rearward movement developed, the aircraft fell several aircraft lengths behind the leader and the airspeed dropped more than 20 knots below the formation airspeed with no timely power restoration. The IP took the controls and restored power to arrest the separation.
texts.1: SP, due to a power reduction not adapted to the climb, allowed excessive rearward movement during the position change. The aircraft moved beyond one aircraft length aft and the airspeed reached 20 knots below the formation airspeed, with the trend stopped only after verbal indications from the IP. The rejoin to the new side was completed well behind the expected timing.
texts.2: SP, due to a power reduction sized as for level flight while the formation was climbing, generated more rearward movement than the crossing required. Airspeed decayed between 10 and 20 knots below the formation airspeed and the spacing approached one aircraft length. SP recognized the growing separation on the leader's aspect, restored power in time and completed the crossing without any intervention.
texts.3: SP kept the power reduction small during the cross under in the climb, so that the rearward movement stayed no larger than the crossing required. Spacing remained inside one aircraft length and the airspeed deviation stayed inside 10 knots of the formation airspeed. Power was restored at the correct point to stop the aft travel.
texts.4: SP adapted the power reduction to the climb without prompting, using a reduction of only a few percent torque, and the rearward movement remained just sufficient for nose-tail clearance. Airspeed excursion was negligible against the formation airspeed and the spacing stayed well inside one aircraft length. The crossing in the climb was flown with no perceptible change of closure.
texts.marginal: SP completed the cross unders in the climb inside the standards, but the rearward movement was repeatedly larger than needed, with airspeed approaching 10 knots low. The trend indicates that the same power reduction is used regardless of whether the formation is level or climbing. Expected improvement is to keep the power reduction small whenever the cross under is flown in a climb, so that the aft displacement stays at the minimum required.

error_modes.label: Anticipating the power addition required while crossing behind No1

texts.0: SP, due to failing to anticipate the slight power increase normally required while flying across and behind the leader, did not stop the rearward movement once nose-tail clearance had been achieved. The aircraft continued to fall aft through the crossing, ending several aircraft lengths behind with more than 20 knots of airspeed difference from the formation and no usable reference on No1. The IP took the controls to restore power and to rejoin the formation.
texts.1: SP, due to power being added only after the rearward travel was already obvious, did not maintain proper nose-tail separation while crossing behind the leader. The spacing opened to the one aircraft length limit and the airspeed to 20 knots below the formation airspeed, and the trend was arrested only after verbal indications from the IP. The rejoin required a large power addition and a late catch-up.
texts.2: SP, due to reacting to the rearward movement instead of anticipating the power change, did not hold the nose-tail separation constant through the crossing. Spacing drifted toward one aircraft length and airspeed between 10 and 20 knots below the formation airspeed while the aircraft was behind the leader. SP identified the growing distance in good time, added power and re-established the correct separation without any intervention.
texts.3: SP anticipated each power change during the cross under, adding power slightly to stop the rearward movement and again as required while crossing behind the leader. Nose-tail separation stayed at the value established at the start, with spacing inside one aircraft length and airspeed inside 10 knots of the formation airspeed. No large throttle movements were needed at any point.
texts.4: SP anticipated the power changes so precisely that the nose-tail separation remained visibly constant from the moment clearance was established until the rejoin. Airspeed excursion against the formation airspeed was negligible and spacing stayed well inside one aircraft length throughout the crossing. Throttle inputs were small, early and continuous rather than corrective.
texts.marginal: SP maintained nose-tail separation inside the standards, but the power addition behind the leader was repeatedly made after the aft movement had started to grow. Spacing approached one aircraft length on several crossings before power was restored. Expected improvement is to anticipate the slight power increase required while crossing behind No1, so that the separation established at the start is simply held rather than recovered.

error_modes.label: Size of the bank used to create the heading crossing angle

texts.0: SP, due to a large bank change instead of the slight bank needed to create a small HCA, did not control the rate of lateral travel across to the new side. The heading diverged more than 10 degrees from the leader's heading and the aircraft continued to translate laterally well past the intended position on the new side. The IP took the controls to remove the crossing angle and to stop the lateral travel.
texts.1: SP, due to a bank input well beyond the few degrees of heading change the technique calls for, generated an excessive HCA during the cross under. Heading divergence reached 10 degrees and the lateral travel had to be stopped after verbal indications from the IP. The arrival on the new side was achieved only after an opposite correction of similar size.
texts.2: SP, due to a bank larger than required to set a small HCA, crossed to the new side with a lateral rate higher than intended. Heading divergence stayed between 5 and 10 degrees and the aircraft reached the new position with residual lateral movement. SP recognized the excess rate, reduced the crossing angle in time and stabilized without any intervention.
texts.3: SP used a slight bank toward the new side, changing heading by only a few degrees to create a small HCA, then rolled wings-level to fly across and behind the leader. Heading divergence stayed inside 5 degrees and the lateral travel was controlled and predictable. The new position was reached without an opposite correction.
texts.4: SP created an HCA of only a few degrees, exactly matched to the lateral distance to be covered, and the crossing developed as one continuous and unhurried translation. Heading divergence from the formation heading was negligible and the aircraft stopped laterally exactly on the new position. Pitch and bank changes remained small throughout.
texts.marginal: SP kept the crossing angles inside the standards, but the initial bank was repeatedly larger than the small HCA the technique describes, with divergence approaching 5 degrees. The result each time was a lateral rate that had to be reduced before arrival on the new side. Expected improvement is to make small pitch and bank changes and to size the HCA to the lateral distance actually required.

error_modes.label: Use of the canopy bow on the elevator trailing edge as nose-tail reference

texts.0: SP, due to not using the nose-tail reference of the canopy bow superimposed on the trailing edge of No1's elevator, did not verify the clearance before moving back and down below the leader's POM. The crossing was started with the aircraft still displaced forward of that reference and the separation from No1 reduced to less than 10 feet during the lateral travel. The IP took the controls to open the separation and to re-establish the position.
texts.1: SP, due to judging the nose-tail position on general impression rather than on the canopy bow and elevator trailing edge reference, crossed behind the leader with less clearance than the technique requires. The separation from No1 reached the 10 feet limit and was opened only after verbal indications from the IP. The aircraft was repositioned below the leader's POM late in the sequence.
texts.2: SP, due to checking the canopy bow against the elevator trailing edge only after the crossing had begun, moved back and down below the leader's POM with the clearance not yet confirmed. The separation from No1 remained above 10 feet but with less margin than intended and the crossing had to be slowed. SP re-established the reference in good time and completed the position change without any intervention.
texts.3: SP established the nose-tail reference before crossing, with the canopy bow appearing superimposed on the trailing edge of No1's elevator, and moved back and down below the leader's POM. The clearance was confirmed visually before any lateral travel and the separation from No1 stayed clearly greater than 10 feet. The crossing was flown with the reference held stable.
texts.4: SP used the canopy bow on the elevator trailing edge as a continuous reference, so that the nose-tail geometry was known at every point of the cross under. Clearance below the leader's POM was established first and the separation from No1 remained far greater than the 10 feet minimum. The reference was regained immediately on the new side with no re-assessment needed.
texts.marginal: SP crossed with acceptable clearance, but the canopy bow was repeatedly only approximately aligned with No1's elevator trailing edge before the lateral travel began. Separation stayed inside the standards while the margin behind the leader was consistently on the small side. Expected improvement is to confirm the nose-tail reference explicitly before moving back and down below the leader's POM on every cross under.

error_modes.label: Power reduction on arrival in the position on the new side

texts.0: SP, due to a late power reduction after adding power to move forward and up into position, did not stabilize on the new side and overshot the position. The aircraft continued forward and up through the formation reference, closing to less than 10 feet from No1 and climbing more than 300 feet above the formation altitude before the movement was arrested. The IP took the controls to stop the closure and to re-establish the formation position.
texts.1: SP, due to leaving the power addition in beyond the point where the position was reached, did not arrest the forward and upward movement at the correct time. The aircraft went through the position with closure toward No1 and a climb reaching 300 feet above the formation altitude, reduced only after verbal indications from the IP. Stabilization on the new side required a second correction in both power and pitch.
texts.2: SP, due to a power reduction applied after arrival instead of just before it, ended the crossing with residual forward and upward movement. The overshoot in the vertical stayed between 150 and 300 feet above the formation altitude and the closure toward No1 had to be stopped. SP recognized the movement, reduced power and settled into the position in time without any intervention.
texts.3: SP added power to move forward and up into the new position and reduced power in time to stabilize there. The arrival was contained inside 150 feet of the formation altitude with separation from No1 well above 10 feet and no forward overshoot. The position was held from the moment of arrival.
texts.4: SP timed the power reduction so that the aircraft arrived in the position with the residual movement already zero. Vertical excursion at arrival was negligible against the formation altitude and the lateral and longitudinal references were correct at the first attempt. No further throttle correction was required after stabilization on the new side.
texts.marginal: SP stabilized on the new side inside the standards, but the power reduction was repeatedly made at arrival rather than in anticipation of it. Each crossing ended with a small forward and upward overshoot that had to be taken out, with vertical excursion approaching 150 feet. Expected improvement is to begin the power reduction before the position is reached, so that the aircraft arrives already stabilized.

error_modes.label: Nose-tail separation while inspecting No1 during the BD check crossunder

texts.0: SP, due to attention being concentrated on the inspection for damage, leaks and missing panels, did not maintain nose-tail separation while crossing under to the other side of No1. The aircraft drifted forward out of the cleared geometry and approached No1 closer than 10 feet with the scan still on the leader's structure. The IP took the controls to open the separation and to terminate the check.
texts.1: SP, due to the inspection task displacing the formation scan, did not hold nose-tail separation during the BD check crossunder. The clearance behind the leader reduced to the 10 feet limit and was recovered only after verbal indications from the IP. The inspection of the second side had to be repeated after the position was re-established.
texts.2: SP, due to dwelling on the leader's wing while repositioning, allowed the nose-tail separation to reduce during the cross under of the BD check. The clearance remained above 10 feet but with a visibly reducing margin as the scan stayed on the inspection. SP interrupted the inspection, re-established the separation in time and completed the check without any intervention.
texts.3: SP maintained nose-tail separation throughout the BD check crossunder while inspecting No1 for damage, leaks, missing panels and irregularities. The scan alternated between the inspection and the formation references, so that spacing stayed inside one aircraft length and separation clearly above 10 feet. The check was completed on both sides and the original position was regained.
texts.4: SP inspected No1 in detail on both sides while the nose-tail geometry remained visibly constant throughout the repositioning. Separation was maintained far above the 10 feet minimum and the aircraft returned to the formation position from which the check was initiated with no correction required. The result of the check was passed without any degradation of the formation position.
texts.marginal: SP kept the separation inside the standards during the BD check, but the nose-tail margin reduced each time the inspection scan was held on the leader for longer periods. The position was always recovered, yet the trend shows the formation scan being suspended while inspecting. Expected improvement is to keep the inspection in short segments so that nose-tail separation is monitored continuously through the crossunder.

error_modes.label: Correcting excessive spacing that develops behind No1 after the crossing

texts.0: SP, due to attempting to correct excessive spacing forward with power alone from directly behind and below the leader, did not recognize the closure rate that developed. The aircraft came out of the excess spacing with an uncontrolled overtake and closed to less than 10 feet from No1 with no lateral offset from which to judge the closure. The IP took the controls to stop the overtake and to re-establish separation.
texts.1: SP, due to correcting the excessive spacing with power only, without establishing a small amount of lead pursuit in the turn, did not control the closure back into position. The separation from No1 reduced to the 10 feet limit before the overtake was arrested, and only after verbal indications from the IP. The final positioning was achieved with a large power reduction late in the correction.
texts.2: SP, due to relying mainly on power to close the excessive spacing from directly astern, recognized the closure rate later than required. The overtake had to be broken with a marked power reduction, with the separation from No1 reduced well below the intended margin although above 10 feet. SP established a lateral offset in time to judge the closure and completed the correction without any intervention.
texts.3: SP corrected the excessive spacing by adding power together with a small amount of lead pursuit in the turn, and by moving off to one side when wings-level to obtain a better visual perspective of No1. Closure was recognized early, the aircraft returned inside one aircraft length and the separation from No1 stayed well above 10 feet. The correction was completed with a single, controlled power cycle.
texts.4: SP treated the excessive spacing with the correct technique from the outset, combining a small power addition with a slight lead pursuit and a lateral perspective on No1. Closure was continuously visible and the return to position was made with negligible overtake and no reduction of the safety margin. The correct spacing was regained without any subsequent adjustment.
texts.marginal: SP recovered the correct spacing inside the standards, but the first correction was repeatedly attempted with power alone from directly astern before an offset was taken. Closure was recognized late on each occasion, leaving less margin than intended on the return to position. Expected improvement is to add power together with a small amount of lead pursuit, or to move off to one side when wings-level, whenever excessive spacing develops.
